docs.title: Home

docs.text: Education is a public good FreeCampus began with a simple conviction: access to excellent learning materials should not depend on where you live, what you earn, or whether you belong to an institution. We bring together learners, educators, subject experts, editors, designers, and developers to create thoughtful materials across disciplines. Our work takes shape through two separate projects with complementary purposes: FreeCampus Community Courses and FreeCampus App . FreeCampus Community Courses FreeCampus Community Courses is our community effort to create and maintain open courses. Contributors develop explanations, examples, practical activities, and exercises that help people study independently, at their own pace. Our ambition is to expand learning opportunities for millions of people worldwide, including across Latin America and Africa. By making high-quality materials developed and reviewed by experts freely accessible, we aim to help learners build skills, pursue new opportunities, and use what they learn to make a difference in their communities and the wider world. The courses are published as public static web pages: lightweight course websites you can read directly in your browser. They include a few quizzes and learning tools to help you check your understanding and put ideas into practice. The tools available vary by course; suitable programming lessons may also offer notebooks you can run in Google Colab. These courses are learning resources in their own right. You can follow their lessons without joining the App or paying for a subscription. Downloadable editions, where available, provide another way to study away from the website. All community activities are unpaid volunteer work. Contributors improve the materials through corrections, new examples, review, and translations. Reuse and adaptation follow each course's license, with credit to the original contributors. Explore the community courses → FreeCampus App FreeCampus App is a separate commercial learning platform in development that builds courses on top of selected community courses. It uses those open materials as a foundation and adds a richer learning experience around them. Its purpose is to help learners make better use of their study time, understand what they have learned, and decide what to work on next. The experience is being designed to connect explanations with purposeful practice, feedback, and opportunities to apply knowledge beyond the lesson. For example, a learner studying a programming concept could move from reading an explanation to solving a challenge, understanding a mistake, and using the concept in a larger project. Planned capabilities include structured learning paths, progress tracking across devices, and deeper practice and assessment. These describe the App's direction, rather than features already available to learners. We are designing primarily for smartphone users, with accessibility and efficient loading in mind. The goal is to help learners build confidence and practical skills, including those studying with limited connectivity or without a computer. Activities that require a computer should be clearly identified. How the two projects fit together Community Courses creates the open learning foundation. The App builds an enhanced learning experience around selected courses from that foundation. They share an educational mission while serving different needs. For independent study: Community Courses provides public lessons, exercises, and lightweight learning tools directly on the web. For more guided learning: The App is being developed to bring selected materials together with structured practice, feedback, and progress tracking. For open access: Community materials remain freely available on their public course websites, independently of App accounts, subscriptions, or participation. For sustainability: The App model includes a free tier and paid tiers. The App team manages its income for App operations and development; community participation does not provide a share of that revenue. The App team may separately contract authors, translators, managers, and other supporters for specific paid tasks. These contracts belong to the App project and are distinct from unpaid community activities. Community participation does not grant decision-making authority in the App or guarantee that a course will have an App version. Any course adapted for the App must have a license that permits the intended use, and its contributors and original sources must be credited. You can use the community courses whether or not you choose to use the App. Our principles 01 Open by default Materials should be available without fees, artificial scarcity, or hidden conditions. 02 Rigorous and humane We value accuracy and depth, expressed with clarity and respect for the learner. 03 Built together Many perspectives make stronger resources. Constructive review is part of authorship. 04 Always improving An open course is never finished. It evolves as knowledge and its community grow. Join the community Our Community Guide explains how authors, translators, reviewers, learners, developers, and community helpers can participate, what to expect, and how licensing and App collaborations work. A campus without gates Educators and practitioners can help shape our courses through the Instructor Network , contributing lessons, practical activities, and thoughtful review. Our public community courses have no admissions process or prescribed pace. You are welcome whether you are meeting a subject for the first time, returning after years away, or helping someone else understand it more deeply. Help improve a course →

docs.text: Two projects, different purposes FreeCampus Community Courses We believe everyone should have access to high-quality learning materials. The community creates open courses to support learners in their learning journey, freely available as static web pages with explanations, practice, quizzes, and learning tools. Our ambition is to expand learning opportunities for millions of people worldwide, including across Latin America and Africa. By making high-quality materials developed and reviewed by experts freely accessible, we aim to help learners build skills, pursue new opportunities, and use what they learn to make a difference in their communities and the wider world. Contributors work together to improve these public resources for their own educational value. The courses remain available independently of the App, without an App account, subscription, or commitment to use it. FreeCampus App The App is a separate commercial project in development. It is designed to help learners go beyond course materials through a richer learning experience, with guided practice, feedback, progress tracking, and projects. Its model includes a free tier and paid tiers; these describe the planned offering, not features already available. The App team manages its development, organization, and income. App revenue supports the App's operation and development and is not a shared community revenue fund. The App team may also commission specific tasks through its own paid contracts, including course creation, updates, and translations. Both projects support learning, but their responsibilities, resources, and ways of working differ. The community focuses on access to open materials; the App focuses on the learning services built around selected materials. Read more about both projects . Community participation and the App All activities within FreeCampus Community Courses are unpaid volunteer work in support of freely accessible education. Community participation does not provide compensation, royalties, a share of App revenue, or a promise that materials will be included in the App. Community contributors help shape the open courses through proposals, discussion, and review. Participation does not grant authority over the App's roadmap, development, or organization; those decisions belong to the App team. You are welcome to contribute to the community without taking part in the App. Your contribution has value as an open learning resource whether or not an App version is ever created. Where materials are reused, their licenses, ownership, and attribution requirements continue to apply. Find your role You can combine roles. Start small and discuss larger contributions with the maintainers before beginning. Authors and course designers Create lessons, examples, exercises, quizzes, or projects. For a new course, propose its audience, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and outline first. Follow the existing course format, include useful feedback, and check examples. Consider phone users and identify activities requiring a computer. Use the Course Author Guide to organize journeys, courses, milestones, units, and lessons. It also explains ungraded practice and progress stored only in the learner's browser on the same device. Authors and maintainers discuss scope, attribution, and maintenance as part of editorial and technical review. Explore the Instructor Network . Translators Translate lessons, exercises, quiz feedback, and supporting instructions. Agree on the language, locale, source version, and file structure first. Preserve attribution, keep code working, and have translations checked for language and subject accuracy. Coordinate review and publication with course maintainers, including how future source changes will be tracked. Reviewers and editors Check accuracy, clarity, learning progression, assessments, or accessibility. Point to the specific lesson, explain the issue, and suggest an improvement. Test exercises and feedback, including incorrect answers. Discuss improvements constructively with authors and maintainers. You can review a single lesson without taking responsibility for the entire course. Learners and testers Report confusing explanations, broken links, missing prerequisites, or exercises that fail. Share the lesson URL, what you expected, and what happened. Include your device when relevant and remove personal information from examples or screenshots. Your feedback helps improve self-paced courses. Individual tutoring and fixed response times are not part of the community offering. Developers and designers Improve websites, notebooks, quizzes, build tools, documentation, or accessibility. Read repository instructions, explain the learner problem, and validate your changes. Favor mobile usability and efficient loading; discuss new services or data collection first. Discuss technical choices and maintenance with the project maintainers. App development requires its own agreed scope and access. Community helpers Welcome newcomers, answer questions, facilitate study discussions, or propose activities. Help learners understand the reasoning and respect different backgrounds and available study time. Agree on responsibilities for ongoing activities or moderation, including schedules and support commitments, before announcing them. How to contribute Choose a project. Browse the subjects and GitHub repositories . Read the project's instructions, license, and open issues. Propose a focused change. Small fixes can go directly to a pull request. For larger work, open an issue with the audience, deliverable, sources, and your availability. Submit and review. Follow the course format, check your work, and explain what changed. Maintainers review submissions and may request revisions before publication. Agree on the handoff. Record attribution, remaining tasks, and any maintenance commitment. Let maintainers know if your availability changes. For a new course or a general question, open an issue in the website repository . Learner feedback can be submitted as an issue without a pull request. Working together We aim to provide clear guidance, constructive review, and recognition through contributor records, acknowledgments, or course credits. Discuss your preferred public name and attribution when submitting work. Publication depends on quality, suitability, licensing, and maintenance capacity. Review timing varies. Choose a contribution you can sustain; ongoing responsibilities should be agreed explicitly. Licenses and credit Check each resource. Read the repository's LICENSE and any separate notices for images, datasets, code, or other assets. Free access alone does not grant reuse rights. Contribute material you can share. Identify sources and permission restrictions. Resolve third-party rights before submission; ask maintainers when terms are unclear. Preserve ownership and attribution. Contributing does not by itself transfer copyright. Retain required notices, credit contributors, and link to original sources when adapting materials. Check App reuse. An App course can adapt community material only when the license permits the intended use, including commercial adaptation, or additional permission is obtained. Public community materials remain open independently of the App. The website , Python , and Mathematics repositories currently publish BSD 3-Clause license files. Follow their actual terms, including required notices and restrictions on implied endorsement, and check for separately licensed assets. This guide does not change those licenses or set the terms for all App materials and software. Separate contracts with the App team The App team may independently contract authors, translators, managers, and other supporters from the community for specific tasks. These may include creating or updating courses, translating materials, coordinating work, teaching, or mentoring, depending on the App's needs and budget. These are paid contracts with the App project, separate from community volunteering. They do not turn community activities into paid work or create a right to payment for previous volunteer contributions. Community members are free to accept or decline an invitation; participation does not guarantee a contract. Each App contract needs an agreement covering scope, compensation, schedule, rights, attribution, and maintenance. Teaching and mentoring also need agreed hours, time zones, and support expectations. You can discuss an opportunity without committing to unpaid preparation or accepting a contract. Introduce your idea ↗

docs.text: This guide is for authors of FreeCampus Community Courses , the freely accessible public learning materials. Community authoring is unpaid volunteer work. Read the Community Guide for contribution steps, licensing, credit, and the separate relationship with the App. Use the Lesson Editorial Guidelines to write individual lessons and review them before submission. Choose the learning structure Journey A FreeCampus Learning Journey , or Journey for short, groups two or more related courses in the same community repository. A repository with one course can present it as a standalone course. A learning path is a suggested route through a Journey. For example, the Python Journey starts with Python Foundations and offers paths into software development and scientific computing. See the FreeCampus Python repository . When a large course would be easier to follow in smaller parts, split it into focused courses and keep them together as a Journey. Give each course its own audience and learning outcomes. On the Journey page, show where to start, what each course requires, and what learners can take next. Reserve program for offerings with formal enrollment or completion requirements. Course A course develops a defined set of skills and must be organized into one or more milestones . Each milestone contains units, and each unit contains lessons. Milestone A milestone contains one or more units and must include a milestone challenge . Use the challenge to bring together what learners practiced across that milestone's units. Explain the outcome learners are working toward and how the units prepare them for it. Unit A unit groups related lessons around a focused topic or outcome. Every unit must include a unit challenge to combine what learners practiced in those lessons. Lesson A lesson introduces and practices a manageable part of a topic. Lessons usually do not have a dedicated challenge. Instead, check understanding through short quizzes, puzzles, worked examples, reflection questions, interactive exercises, or Google Colab notebooks where appropriate. Choose activities that fit the subject and explain what learners should notice, try, or understand. Not every lesson needs every activity type. Write course content in Quarto Write all course content in Quarto ( .qmd ). For lessons configured for Colab, the publishing pipeline generates a Jupyter notebook ( .ipynb ) from the lesson source and renders an Open this lesson in Google Colab link on the lesson page. Follow the course repository’s conventions for notebook metadata and the shared Colab link. Make edits in the .qmd source so the published page and notebook reflect the same lesson. The first Python Foundations lesson shows the notebook metadata and link include in context. Example outline This is an illustrative structure, not a required repository folder layout: Journey: Practical Programming groups two courses: Programming Foundations and Data Automation . The Foundations course includes this milestone: Milestone: Work with everyday data Unit: Values and variables Lesson: Explore values, with a prediction puzzle. Lesson: Use variables, with a Google Colab exercise. Unit challenge: Create a simple expense summary. Unit: Collections Lesson: Work with lists, with short understanding checks. Lesson: Use dictionaries, with guided practice. Unit challenge: Organize a small inventory using lists and dictionaries. Milestone challenge: Combine variables and collections to summarize a small dataset. The Automation course follows the same required structure: milestones with milestone challenges, and units with lessons and unit challenges. Follow the repository's existing file conventions. Discuss structural changes with maintainers before reorganizing published content or changing lesson URLs. Design practice without grades Community courses are not graded. Lesson activities, unit challenges, and milestone challenges help learners practice and check their own understanding; they are not graded examinations. Milestone and unit challenges are required parts of the course structure and remain ungraded. For each activity or challenge: State the goal and provide clear instructions, prerequisites, and any starter files or data. Include useful feedback, hints, expected behavior, explanations, or a suggested solution so learners can review their work. Use quizzes or automated checks for learning feedback, without turning their results into a course grade or a pass requirement. Make activities readable on a phone and identify work that needs a computer or an external tool such as Google Colab. Progress indicators show where a learner has reached. They are not grades or verified evidence of mastery. Do not promise instructor grading or individual review as part of a community course. Explain browser-local progress Community course progress is stored locally in the learner's web browser. It is limited to the same browser and browser profile on the same device ; it does not automatically synchronize to another device or browser. Clearing the site's browser data can remove saved progress. Private browsing may discard it when the session ends. Do not describe this tracking as a cloud backup or imply that signing into the separate App restores community-course progress. Include a short explanation near the course introduction or progress controls, for example: This course is ungraded. Your progress is saved in this browser on this device. It does not sync across devices and may be lost if you clear the site's browser data. These progress and grading rules describe Community Courses. The separate App has its own product design and implementation. Before submitting Explain the audience, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and suggested learning order. Use journey, course, milestone, unit, and lesson consistently. Organize every course into milestones and include a milestone challenge in each milestone. Include lessons and a unit challenge in every unit. Check that activities have useful feedback and that code, notebook links, and supporting files work. State the ungraded nature of the course and the limits of browser-local progress. Preserve required licenses and contributor credit, and follow the repository's review and build instructions. Discuss a course idea ↗

docs.text: A unit groups related lessons around a focused topic or outcome. Every unit must include a unit challenge to combine what learners practiced in those lessons.
docs.title: Unit

docs.text: A lesson introduces and practices a manageable part of a topic. Lessons usually do not have a dedicated challenge. Instead, check understanding through short quizzes, puzzles, worked examples, reflection questions, interactive exercises, or Google Colab notebooks where appropriate. Choose activities that fit the subject and explain what learners should notice, try, or understand. Not every lesson needs every activity type.
docs.title: Lesson

docs.text: Write all course content in Quarto ( .qmd ). For lessons configured for Colab, the publishing pipeline generates a Jupyter notebook ( .ipynb ) from the lesson source and renders an Open this lesson in Google Colab link on the lesson page. Follow the course repository’s conventions for notebook metadata and the shared Colab link. Make edits in the .qmd source so the published page and notebook reflect the same lesson. The first Python Foundations lesson shows the notebook metadata and link include in context.
docs.title: Write course content in Quarto

docs.text: This is an illustrative structure, not a required repository folder layout: Journey: Practical Programming groups two courses: Programming Foundations and Data Automation . The Foundations course includes this milestone: Milestone: Work with everyday data Unit: Values and variables Lesson: Explore values, with a prediction puzzle. Lesson: Use variables, with a Google Colab exercise. Unit challenge: Create a simple expense summary. Unit: Collections Lesson: Work with lists, with short understanding checks. Lesson: Use dictionaries, with guided practice. Unit challenge: Organize a small inventory using lists and dictionaries. Milestone challenge: Combine variables and collections to summarize a small dataset. The Automation course follows the same required structure: milestones with milestone challenges, and units with lessons and unit challenges. Follow the repository's existing file conventions. Discuss structural changes with maintainers before reorganizing published content or changing lesson URLs.
docs.title: Example outline

docs.text: Community courses are not graded. Lesson activities, unit challenges, and milestone challenges help learners practice and check their own understanding; they are not graded examinations. Milestone and unit challenges are required parts of the course structure and remain ungraded. For each activity or challenge: State the goal and provide clear instructions, prerequisites, and any starter files or data. Include useful feedback, hints, expected behavior, explanations, or a suggested solution so learners can review their work. Use quizzes or automated checks for learning feedback, without turning their results into a course grade or a pass requirement. Make activities readable on a phone and identify work that needs a computer or an external tool such as Google Colab. Progress indicators show where a learner has reached. They are not grades or verified evidence of mastery. Do not promise instructor grading or individual review as part of a community course.
docs.title: Design practice without grades

docs.text: Community course progress is stored locally in the learner's web browser. It is limited to the same browser and browser profile on the same device ; it does not automatically synchronize to another device or browser. Clearing the site's browser data can remove saved progress. Private browsing may discard it when the session ends. Do not describe this tracking as a cloud backup or imply that signing into the separate App restores community-course progress. Include a short explanation near the course introduction or progress controls, for example: This course is ungraded. Your progress is saved in this browser on this device. It does not sync across devices and may be lost if you clear the site's browser data. These progress and grading rules describe Community Courses. The separate App has its own product design and implementation.
docs.title: Explain browser-local progress

docs.text: Explain the audience, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and suggested learning order. Use journey, course, milestone, unit, and lesson consistently. Organize every course into milestones and include a milestone challenge in each milestone. Include lessons and a unit challenge in every unit. Check that activities have useful feedback and that code, notebook links, and supporting files work. State the ungraded nature of the course and the limits of browser-local progress. Preserve required licenses and contributor credit, and follow the repository's review and build instructions. Discuss a course idea ↗
docs.title: Before submitting

docs.text: Teach beyond the classroom The FreeCampus Instructor Network brings together educators and practitioners who want to help create rigorous, freely accessible learning materials. Whether you teach in a classroom, mentor a team, or explain ideas through open projects, your experience can help more people learn. Affiliated instructors volunteer with the community on lessons, exercises, and course review. All community activities are unpaid. The separate App team may offer paid contracts for specific tasks; community authorship does not guarantee a contract or inclusion in the App. Start with a subject you know well and a contribution you can sustain. Start a conversation → Ways to contribute Create Build a learning path Turn your subject knowledge into clear lessons, worked examples, and a sequence learners can follow. Practice Make ideas tangible Design purposeful exercises, quizzes, and projects that connect explanations to practical understanding. Review Strengthen a course Check accuracy, prerequisites, and learning progression. Help authors make difficult ideas easier to grasp. Adapt Reach more learners Improve accessibility, translate explanations, and bring examples from different communities and contexts. How we work together Begin with a lesson, a review, or a course proposal. Agree on the scope with the project maintainers, then develop the material openly so others can offer feedback and help improve it. Put learners first. State the prerequisites and learning goals, explain ideas clearly, and include meaningful practice. Work in the open. Use the relevant project's contribution guidance and license, and credit the people and sources behind the material. Welcome review. Discuss feedback constructively and check examples and exercises before sharing them. Choose a sustainable scope. Talk with maintainers about the time you can give and how the material will be maintained. For practical guidance on authorship, translations, review, licensing, recognition, and separately contracted App work, read the Community Guide . Meet the instructors Meet the educators and practitioners helping shape FreeCampus. Our instructors bring experience in programming education, course development, and data science training. Founder · Instructor Ivan Ogasawara Ivan creates and develops the FreeCampus Python course, combining lessons, runnable examples, quizzes, debugging exercises, and projects. His educational experience includes work as a Python instructor and AI teaching assistant at The GRAPH Network, and as a teaching assistant at WorldQuant University. He also collaborated as an author on WorldQuant University's new Applied Data Science Lab course. He structures learning materials to help learners build, explain, test, and improve their own programs. Teaching areas Python programming · Software development · Scientific computing Ivan on LinkedIn ↗ Already contributing to a FreeCampus course? Share a short biography, your subject areas, links to your contributions, and any public profile links you would like included when you contact the maintainers. Get involved Browse our subjects and choose an existing course or a topic you would like to propose. Visit the relevant project through the FreeCampus GitHub organization . Open an issue to introduce your proposal; for a new course or a general inquiry, use the website repository . Describe your teaching or practical experience, the learners you want to support, and the contribution you have in mind. Discuss the next step with the maintainers before starting a larger course. You can contribute a small improvement at any time. Visit our contribution guide for other ways to help. Introduce your teaching idea ↗

docs.text: Use these guidelines to write and review lessons for FreeCampus Community Courses. The Course Author Guide explains how lessons fit into units and milestones and how ungraded practice works. Plan the lesson Give the lesson one main outcome. Say what learners will be able to do, using a verb such as explain, compare, calculate, configure, or debug. “Distinguish correlation from causation in a news claim” gives learners a concrete target. Explain why the outcome matters. A short case, question, or use case can show where the idea applies before you introduce the details. State prerequisites and access needs up front. Link to earlier lessons where possible. Say when learners need a computer, a particular operating system, an account, a download, or physical materials. Put examples and practice close to the explanation Introduce the idea. Explain one meaningful idea at a time. Use headings that describe what the learner will do or understand. Show how it works. Place a worked example, case, diagram, or demonstration beside the idea it illustrates. Explain the decisions behind it. Let learners try. Ask them to apply or explain what they learned. Say what to produce and provide feedback they can use on their own, such as a hint, a worked answer, an expected result, or criteria for a well-reasoned response. Repeat this sequence after a meaningful step. A short concept lesson may need one cycle, and a multi-step workflow may need several. Close with a brief recap or a link to the next lesson or challenge when it helps learners continue. Write for a global, mobile-first audience Address the learner directly. Use plain, precise language, short paragraphs, descriptive headings, and numbered steps for procedures. Explain steps that words such as “obviously” or “just” would gloss over. Define unfamiliar terms, acronyms, and symbols when they first matter. Use consistent terminology in explanations, exercises, and feedback. Match interface labels and code identifiers exactly. Give examples that make sense across regions or explain the local context. Include the units, date formats, and currency learners need to interpret the example. Use images, diagrams, and screenshots where they clarify an idea or action. Provide useful alt text for informative images and explain complex visuals in nearby text. Use readable labels and contrast. Identify items by name or position as well as color. Keep commands, code, formulas, and essential instructions available as text. Emojis are optional and should carry no essential meaning on their own. Preview the lesson on a narrow screen. Keep media and downloads small where practical. If an activity requires a computer or a large download, keep the explanation and expected result readable on a phone. Cite sources for quotations, data, and claims that need evidence. Record the source, license, and required credit for reused images, code, and datasets. Label fictional or simplified examples when learners might otherwise read them as evidence. Choose the approach by what learners will do These approaches can be combined. An engineering lesson might introduce a concept, work through a calculation, and use a simulation to check the result. Concepts, theory, and interpretation Define the concept, distinguish it from a related idea, and show where it applies or where it breaks down. When interpretations differ, explain the scope of each view and what evidence supports it. A short prompt to compare, classify, predict, or explain can be enough practice. For open-ended questions, describe what a defensible answer includes and accept multiple well-reasoned answers. For example, after introducing correlation and causation, ask learners to explain whether a study headline supports a causal claim and name one piece of evidence that would strengthen it. Calculation, quantitative reasoning, and proofs State the givens, assumptions, notation, and units where applicable. Explain why each key step in a worked example follows. Show how to check the result using an estimate, a unit check, substitution, or a boundary case. Then change an input or condition and ask learners what changes. In a proof lesson, ask learners to identify where an assumption is used and what happens if it is dropped. Software and tool workflows State the starting point, supported environment, and expected result. Use the actual menu labels, button names, and commands. Note relevant differences across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Use a cropped, readable screenshot when learners need to locate a control or recognize an output. Give the same essential directions in text. For example, in a lesson about an integrated development environment (IDE), show how to select the Python interpreter, run a file, and verify which interpreter ran it. Include a recovery step if the IDE selects a different environment. Labs, fieldwork, and design List materials, conditions, and relevant safety requirements. Explain what learners should measure, record, build, or decide. Provide a sample result or trade-off and show how to recognize a setup or measurement error. When practical, offer sample data or a lower-equipment option that supports the same reasoning. Programming Teach a skill at a time. Introduce the concept, its purpose, and a use case. Explain the library, function, method, class, or parameter when it becomes useful. Show relevant inputs, outputs, or side effects and why the example uses that tool. Link to documentation for details beyond the lesson. Pair short explanations with runnable code. Show the expected output or behavior. Give learners something to predict, run, trace, modify, or debug before moving to another substantial concept. State any setup the example depends on. Use checkpoints to help learners recover. After a meaningful intermediate step, explain what learners should see, why it looks that way, and what to inspect if their result differs. A short text checkpoint can show the expected output or state. When code can check the result reliably, prefer a runnable block with assertions. Give each assertion a message that identifies what failed and what to inspect. Include the expected and actual values when they help learners diagnose the problem. Add short quizzes at meaningful transitions. This is strongly recommended. Ask learners to predict an output, choose an explanation, or identify a likely bug. Explain the reasoning in the feedback, especially when a plausible wrong answer reveals a common misunderstanding. Make practice a small step beyond the example. Keep the target concept and change the dataset, condition, or input. Give a starting point and success criteria. Offer hints before a worked solution, then explain the solution so learners can compare it with their own approach. Model readable, documented code. Use meaningful names and include docstrings for Python functions, methods, and classes written for the lesson. FreeCampus recommends numpydoc or Douki . Use the course’s chosen style consistently and document relevant parameters, return values, exceptions, and side effects. numpydoc style guide · Douki YAML docstring format Use assertions in practice where they give useful feedback. Check behavior and accept different implementations that meet the same requirements. Cover a representative case and a relevant edge case when applicable. For exploratory or visual work, an expected observation may be a better check. These checks support self-review in community lessons. Verify the learner’s execution path. For Colab lessons, use executable cells in the Quarto source and follow the course publishing workflow . Open the generated notebook using the lesson’s Colab link. In a fresh runtime, run setup and examples in order and try the practice and feedback as a learner would. Make dependencies and data loading explicit. Verify local workflows in the environment the lesson specifies. Example programming lesson See how a lesson can teach one skill with runnable examples, text and assertion checkpoints, and short quizzes. The example asks learners to apply the skill to a new record and provides practice checks and a worked answer. Read a Record from CSV, JSON, and YAML (.qmd source) Name activities consistently Checkpoint helps learners verify an intermediate result and recover if it differs. Quiz asks one or more short questions and explains the reasoning behind the answers. Practice applies the current lesson skill. Use Lab for practice with a dedicated notebook, workspace, or hands-on procedure. Unit Challenge combines skills taught in the unit. Milestone Challenge combines skills from the milestone’s units. Use project for what learners build when a challenge has a project deliverable. A lesson can use a running example or a small lab to teach an individual skill. Place larger programming projects in Unit Challenges or Milestone Challenges, after the tools and concepts they depend on have been taught. Link each challenge to the relevant lessons so learners can revisit them. Review checklist Mark each applicable criterion Meets or Revise . Use N/A for criteria outside the lesson’s scope. Resolve items marked Revise before approval. Keep suggestions about recommended practices separate. When requesting a revision, point to the section, explain the problem for the learner, and describe what would resolve it. Outcome and scope. The lesson has an observable outcome, a clear purpose, and any necessary prerequisites or access requirements. Sequence. Ideas build in a usable order, with examples or demonstrations close to the explanations they support. Practice and feedback. Learners can attempt a check aligned with the outcome and understand why their result is sound or what to try if it differs. Language and access. Terms are consistent, instructions and visuals are accessible, and the lesson is readable on a phone. Accuracy and attribution. Claims, examples, expected results, and sources are accurate. Reused material includes the required license information and credit. Lesson approach. The lesson provides the information its activity needs, such as model reasoning for an interpretation, units and assumptions for a calculation, or expected results and recovery steps for a software workflow. Programming. Examples and practice checks work in the stated environment. Checkpoints help learners diagnose likely errors. Authored Python functions, methods, and classes follow the selected docstring convention. Challenge placement. The lesson focuses on its own skills. Any related Unit Challenge or Milestone Challenge uses the correct label and links back to the lessons it draws on. For a review pass, try the main activity before looking at the solution. Make one likely mistake and see whether the feedback helps you recover.
